## **Abstract**

**Background:** Tumor-based endpoints are part of the main endpoint in oncological research, but their evaluation is based on a series of subjective choices, which include the rules used to censor patients and the timing at which tumor progression is recorded and are therefore more prone to bias than more objective endpoint such as Overall Survival (OS). Sensitivity analyses are used to evaluate the robustness of trial results for the different endpoints, but the inclusion of the type of sensitivity analysis is also a subjective choice. Our study aim at compare the results between primary and sensitivity analyses and identify possible pattern of choice.

**Methods:** We extracted the numerical results for all the primary and sensitivity analyses reported in publicly available documents for each trials. We then used these results to compute the ratio of Hazard Ratios (HRs) and of Standard Errors between primary and sensitivity analyses and then analysed the relation of those to ratios to explore the relationship between primary and sensitivity analyses, also investigating the role that the different type of sensitivity analyses and the value of the Hazard Ratios for the primary analysis have in this relationship.

**Results:** The simple linear model showed a relationship between the ratio of standard errors and the ratio of Hazard ratios, but the other models explored did not have significant covariates.also the models accounting for clustering of sensitivity analyses gave results very close to the simple linear model ones.

## Introduction

An essential part of oncological research is based on survival analysis, as one of the main goals is to reduce mortality in patients, as well as increase the time without disease progression [@wilson2015]. Overall survival (OS), defined as the time from randomisation to death, is seen as the gold standard in oncology clinical trials [@gormley2025], as it is easy to measure, since we usually have a precise time for death. It is also very objective, as death is a well-defined endpoint and its measurement cannot be biased by the researcher’s assessment. Moreover, the censoring rules, which are the set of scenarios that describe when a patient will be censored, employed in the analysis of OS tend to be simple and consistent among trials, reducing the possibility of bias. At the same time, OS requires very long follow-up periods and its usefulness is limited in the case of slow-progressing diseases with a long survival expectancy, as there is a high chance of intercurrent events or changes in treatment [@kilickap].

These are some of the reasons why surrogate endpoints based on tumor assessment are widely accepted, even if they are continuous endpoints measured by discrete assessments nd therefore rely on the timing of the investigation [@wilson2015].

The most common tumor-based endpoints are:

-   Progression-Free Survival (PFS), defined as the time from randomisation until the first evidence of disease progression or death[@progress2011].

-   Disease-Free Survival (DFS), defined as the time from randomisation until evidence of disease recurrence [@disease-2011].

-   Event-Free Survival (EFS), defined as the time from randomisation to an event which may include disease progression, discontinuation of the treatment for any reason, or death [@event-fr2011].

-   Relapse-Free Survival (RFS), defined as the length of time after primary treatment that the patient survives without any signs or symptoms of that cancer [@definiti2011].

The choice of tumor-based endpoint depends on the type of tumor studied [@kilickap], but they are all subject to the possibility of bias [@wilson2015]. Therefore, their use is more controversial compared with OS, due to the subjectivity of tumor assessment. These endpoints also rely more on how different scenarios are accounted for as that can affect whether some and until which points some patients are included in the analyses. This means that they are more prone to obtaining different results depending on the type of primary analysis and censoring rules employed [@lesan2024], and, therefore, to bias.

To evaluate how dependent the primary results are on methodological choices and assess their robustness and the potential impact of bias, sensitivity analyses are often employed. These analyses reassess study outcomes with varying methodologies, assumptions, and/or censoring rules. However, the choice of which primary and sensitivity analyses to include in the study remains a subjective one.

This study is the exploratory part of a larger project to evaluate the reproducibility and robustness of the main oncological endpoints. Its main aims are to:

1.  Assess the reproducibility of the main studies that supported European Medicine Agency (EMA) authorisations of indications for oncological drugs.

2.  Evaluate the robustness of the selected studies’ conclusions using different censoring rules.

3.  Analyse, when possible, the difference in results between the primary and the sensitivity analyses to identify possible trends in the choice of primary analyses.

This study focused on this last point, making use of the publicly available results from a sample of oncological randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to investigate the differences between the results obtained in the primary analyses and the ones obtained from the sensitivity analyses, when available.

## Methods

We identified all oncological indications that received a positive opinion from the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) between January 01, 2020 and December 31, 2024. Using the European public assessment reports (EPARs), we then identified 223 RCTs referred to as ‘main studies’.

We used the results of an earlier audit of data sharing by pharmaceutical companies for oncology trials, to calculate the size of the sample needed for our study. This previous paper found that only 34% of trials that supported FDA approval between 2011 and 2021 had accessible IPD [@hopkins2023]. We used 34% as the expected proportion of reproducible trials and 12% as the half-width of the 95% CI and obtained 60 trials as required sample size for our study. Therefore we selected 60 RCTs using the sampling function \texttt{sample()} implemented in R, setting a seed for computational reproducibility.

During the review of the documents of the selected trials, it was noticed that two of them did not report any analyses for neither OS nor any tumor based endpoint. They were removed from the sample and two more were randomly selected using the same function and seed but removing the already selected studies from the pool of selectable studies.

For each selected RCT, we requested the relevant document to reanalyze the original results.

At the same time we have also collected the publicly available information on the type of primary and sensitivity analyses conducted in each RCT through EPARs, journal articles and their supplementary materials, Protocols and SAPs; extracting their results in terms of Hazard Ratios (HRs) and confidence intervals (CIs) for OS and tumor-based endpoints, for each analysis in each RCT.

### Data extraction

We created an [spreadsheet](https://uniren1-my.sharepoint.com/:x:/g/personal/giulia_varvara_univ-rennes_fr/EYIBktM27lhIvCf4wRn-030BDRcOL2O7wJAb2NL6Ws71Hw?e=XwaLyy) containing, for each RCT, information about the main time-to-event endpoint analysed, the type of primary and sensitivity analyses reported in any of the publicly available documents (EPARs, publications and their supplementary materials), the censoring rules employed and the values for HRs, lower and upper bounds of the Confidence Intervals, $p$-value and, when possible, the median survival time.

For simplification, all the different tumor-based endpoints such as Progression-Free Survival (PFS), Disease-Free Survival (DFS), Relapse-Free Survival (RFS) etc. were grouped under the label of Tumor-Based Endpoint (TBE) in our analyses. Then we proceeded to use the extracted information to compare the results from the primary analyses with the ones obtained in the sensitivity analyses in each RCT.

```{r Read data and split into trials, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
#install.packages("readxl")
library(readxl)
#install.packages('stringr')
library(stringr)
#remotes::install_github(repo = "EBPI-Biostatistics/biostatUZH", build_vignettes = FALSE)
library(biostatUZH)

data=read_excel("Sensitivity and censoring summary.xlsx", sheet = "Analysis results")
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)

# Split type of sensitivity analyses strings into a character vector
#split_cats <- strsplit(data$`Type of sensitivity analysis`, ", ")
#all_cats <- sort(unique(unlist(split_cats)))

all_cats <- sort(unique(unlist(data$`Type of sensitivity analysis`)))


# Group and split the data frame creating one object per NCT
split_df_grouped <- data %>%
  group_by(NCT) %>%
  group_split()
```

Sensitivity analyses were then divided into three categories according to the type of sensitivity analysis. Sensitivity analyses were categorised as relative to "Censoring rules" when the main difference with the primary analysis was the set of rules defining in which situations patients should be censored and how their data should be included in the analysis. They were defined as changes in "Population" when the sensitivity analysis was focusing on a different population or a subset of the primary analysis's population. Finally, they were classified as differing in "Methods" when different types of analysis, stratification or evaluation of tumor growth were employed.

The number of sensitivity analyses per category for each point is reported in *Table* \@ref(tab:Table-categories), from which it is also possible to see the same sensitivity analyses fell under more than one category.

```{r Compute ratios, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
med_sens_OS=c()
med_sens_TBE=c()
comparisons=list()

for (y in seq_along(split_df_grouped)) { #For each NCT
  NCT1 <- split_df_grouped[[y]] 
  NCT_name <- unique(NCT1$NCT)
  #Identify Primary and Sensitivity analyses
  NCT1=cbind(NCT1[,1:2], str_split_fixed(NCT1$Analysis, ", ",2), NCT1[,4:ncol(NCT1)]) #Split third column in endpoint and analysis (sensitivity or primary)
  NCT1=NCT1 %>% rename("Endpoint" = "1", "Analysis" = "2")
  endpoints=unique(NCT1$Endpoint) 
  #Divide RCT's results according to the endpoint
  groups=NCT1 %>% 
    group_by(Endpoint)%>%
    group_split()
  NCT_comp=list()
  
  for(i in 1:length(groups)){ #For each endpoint
    gg=groups[[i]]
    end=unique(gg$Endpoint)
    kk=which(grepl("Primary", gg[["Analysis"]])) #Identify the primary analysis
    ref_HR=as.numeric(gg[kk,"HR"])
    Analysis= gg[-kk,"Analysis"]#Transform it in numeric value
    if(is.na(ref_HR)){
      print(paste(NCT_name, end,gg$Analysis[kk], " reported as:", gg[kk,"HR"])) #If the HR is not a numeric value, print what is reported
    }
    ref_LB=as.numeric(gg[kk,"CI Lower bound"])
    ref_UB=as.numeric(gg[kk,"CI upper bound"])
    if(is.na(ref_LB)| is.na(ref_UB)){ #If there are not enough numerical information for the CI, report it
      print(paste(NCT_name, end,gg$Analysis[kk], " no CI information"))
    }
    #Save the sensitivity analysis results in different vectors
    sens_HR=as.numeric(unlist(gg[-kk,"HR"]))
    sens_LB=as.numeric(unlist(gg[-kk,"CI Lower bound"]))
    sens_UB=as.numeric(unlist(gg[-kk,"CI upper bound"]))
    sens_type=gg[-kk, "Type of sensitivity analysis"]
    
    #Record which sensitivity analysis had no numerical value
    h_na=which(is.na(sens_HR))
    lb_na=which(is.na(sens_LB))
    ub_na=which(is.na(sens_UB))
    if(length(h_na)!=0 | length(sens_HR)==0){ #If the HR are reported but not numerically, print the reported statement
      cc=which(is.na(as.numeric(gg$HR)))
      print(paste(NCT_name, end,gg$Analysis[cc], "HR reported as:", gg$HR[cc]))
      #sens_HR=sens_HR[-h_na] #Remove non numerical values from the vector of values
    }
    if(length(lb_na)!=0 | length(ub_na)!=0 |length(sens_LB)==0| length(sens_UB)==0){ #Repeat for the CIs
      ww=unique(c(which(is.na(gg$`CI Lower bound`)),which(is.na(gg$`CI upper bound`))))
      print(paste(NCT_name, end,gg$Analysis[ww], " no CI information"))
      #sens_LB=sens_LB[-c(lb_na,ub_na)]
      #sens_UB=sens_UB[-c(lb_na,ub_na)]
      
    }
    # if(!is_empty(unique(c(h_na, ub_na, lb_na)))){
    #   sens_type=sens_type[-unique(c(h_na, ub_na, lb_na)),]
    # }

  
#Once all the non usable instances have been removed, compare log(HR)s of the sensitivity analyses to the one of the primary one.
# Safe subset: only remove NA indices if h_na is valid (not 0 and not empty)
  valid_HR <- sens_HR
  if (length(h_na) > 0 && all(h_na != 0)) valid_HR[h_na] <- NA

  if (!is.na(ref_HR) & sum(!is.na(valid_HR)) != 0)  { #Check that there are sensitivity analyses to compare
    ratio_HR <- log(valid_HR / ref_HR)
  
    if (grepl("OS", end)) {
      med_sens_OS <- c(med_sens_OS, length(valid_HR)) #Count how many sensitivity analyses for OS for RCT
    }
    if (grepl("FS", end)) { #Count how many sensitivity analyses for TBE for RCT
      med_sens_TBE <- c(med_sens_TBE, length(valid_HR))
    }
  
  } else { #If no possible comparison to make record it
  
    if (grepl("OS", end)) {
      if (length(sens_HR) != 0 & length(valid_HR) == 0) {  # HRs exist but all are NA
        med_sens_OS <- c(med_sens_OS, NA)
      }
      if (length(sens_HR) == 0) {                           # No HRs at all
        med_sens_OS <- c(med_sens_OS, 0)
      }
    }
  
    if (grepl("FS", end)) {
      if (length(sens_HR) != 0 & length(valid_HR) == 0) {  # HRs exist but all are NA
        med_sens_TBE <- c(med_sens_TBE, NA)
      }
      if (length(sens_HR) == 0) {                           # No HRs at all
        med_sens_TBE <- c(med_sens_TBE, 0)
      }
    }
  
  ratio_HR <- paste(NCT_name, "No possible HR comparison for ", end)
}
    CI_se_ref <- CI_se_sens <- c()

# Replace NAs in place to keep alignment
  valid_LB <- sens_LB
  valid_UB <- sens_UB
  if (length(lb_na) > 0 && all(lb_na != 0)) valid_LB[lb_na] <- NA
  if (length(ub_na) > 0 && all(ub_na != 0)) valid_UB[ub_na] <- NA

  if (!is.na(ref_LB) & !is.na(ref_UB)) {
    CI_se_ref <- ci2se(ref_LB, ref_UB, conf.level = 0.95, ratio = TRUE)
  
    if (sum(!is.na(valid_LB)) != 0 & sum(!is.na(valid_UB)) != 0) {
    
      # Compute ci2se only on non-NA positions
      CI_se_sens <- rep(NA, length(valid_LB))  # pre-fill with NAs to keep alignment
      non_na_idx <- which(!is.na(valid_LB) & !is.na(valid_UB))  # valid positions
    
      CI_se_sens[non_na_idx] <- ci2se(valid_LB[non_na_idx], valid_UB[non_na_idx],
                                     conf.level = 0.95, ratio = TRUE)
      # NA positions are already NA from pre-fill
    }
  }
    if(length(CI_se_ref)!=0 & length(CI_se_sens)!=0){ #Calculate ratio of Se if possible
      log_ratio_se=log(CI_se_sens/CI_se_ref)
    }else{
      log_ratio_se=paste(NCT_name, "No possible CI comparison for ",end) #Declare if not possible
      print(log_ratio_se)
    }
    if(nrow(sens_type)>0){
       NCT_comp[[end]]=data.frame(Analysis,log_ratio=ratio_HR, log_se=log_ratio_se, sens_type, ref_HR)
    }else{
      NCT_comp[[end]]=data.frame(log_ratio=ratio_HR, log_se=log_ratio_se, ref_HR)
      }
  }
  comparisons[[NCT_name]]=NCT_comp
}
```

```{r Combine comparisons, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
dif_OS=data.frame()
dif_TBE=data.frame()
x=y=0
for (i in 1:length(comparisons)) {
  ep=names(comparisons[[i]])
  comparisons[[i]]
  ep
  for(j in 1:length(ep)){
    rp=rep(names(comparisons)[i],length(comparisons[[i]][[ep[j]]]$log_ratio))
    res= comparisons[[i]][[ep[j]]] %>% mutate_at(c('log_ratio', 'log_se'), as.numeric)
    res <- data.frame(
      NCT = rp,
      res
    )
    if(ncol(res)<5){
      res[,"Type.of.sensitivity.analysis"]=rep(0,nrow(comparisons[[i]][[ep[j]]]))
       res[,"Analysis"]=rep(0,nrow(comparisons[[i]][[ep[j]]]))
    }
    if(grepl("OS", ep[j])){
      dif_OS=rbind(dif_OS,res)
      }
    if(grepl("FS", ep[j])){
      dif_TBE=rbind(dif_TBE,res)
      }
  }
  
}
#colnames(dif_OS)=colnames(dif_TBE)=c("NCT","HRR", "seR", all_cats)

dif_OS_clean=na.omit(dif_OS)

dif_TBE_clean=na.omit(dif_TBE)
```

                                  levels = c(0, 1),

```{r Table-categories,tab.cap="Type of sensitivity analysis per endpoint", echo=FALSE}
tTBE=table(dif_TBE_clean$Type.of.sensitivity.analysis)
tOS=table(dif_OS_clean$Type.of.sensitivity.analysis)

knitr::kable(t_tot, caption = "Type of sensitivity analysis per endpoint", position = "H")
```

A sensitivity analysis could fall into multiple categories at the same time if it presents difference with the primary analysis in more than one point. For example, the sensitivity analysis of an RCT could change the evaluation method from an Independent Review Committee (IRC) to an Investigator based one, but at the same time focus on the Per-Protocol population instead of the population that the primary analysis was focused on; in this case the sensitivity analysis would be classified as both "Methods" and "Population" based.

We used these data collected from the public records to create forest plots of the results for each RCT, which are available in the [appendix](https://github.com/GVarv/Zurich-project/blob/main/combined_forestplots.pdf).

Then we proceeded to use the extracted information to compare the results from the primary analyses with the ones obtained in the sensitivity analyses in each RCT.

All the files and code used for this project are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/GVarv/Zurich-project)

### Analysis comparison per trial

To identify whether there was any pattern in the choice of primary or sensitivity analysis, we compared the results from each of the reported analyzes retrieving the standard errors of each HR using the \texttt{ci2se} function from the \texttt{biostatUZH} R package and then computed the ratio between the standard errors of the sensitivity analyzes and the one of the primary analyzes. Similarly, we computed the logarithm of the ratio of the HR of the sensitivity analysis over the HR of the primary analysis.

We then examined the distribution of these quantities for each endpoint and, to examine the possibility of a relation between the comparison of HRs and standard error between sensitivity and primary analyzes, we plotted the ratio of the standard errors computed before against the logarithm of the ratio of HRs.

We then modeled the relation between these values for each endpoint using a linear model that only included HR as regression variable as first step; then, since the scatter plot suggested the presence of two different trends, we explore the possibility of different distributions using finite mixture models.

Afterwards, we tested whether the category in which the sensitivity analysis were catagorized beforehand could influence the model results. We added the different categories as a fixed variable in the model. To account for the fact that some sensitivity analyses fell under multiple categories at once, we created 3 dummy variables to indicate the presence or absence of change in each category.

Finally, we expanded the previous models to account for the presence of clustering, as in the dataset, multiple data points come from the same RCT, using a mixed model and compared the results of these different analyses.

## Results

### Sensitivity analysis frequency

The frequency of the number of sensitivity analyses per endpoint. is illustrated by Fig. \@ref(fig:Frequency-plot). This plot only includes the analyses that reported numerical values , but, among the sensitivity analyses described in the public documents we examined, 14 analyses coming from 10 RCTs were described but did not have any results described.

```{r Frequency-plot,fig.cap="Number of sensitivty analyses per endpoint", echo=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

# Combine into a data frame with a group label
df <- data.frame(
  value = c(med_sens_OS, med_sens_TBE),
  group = factor(c(rep("OS", length(med_sens_OS)), rep("TBE", length(med_sens_TBE))))
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_bar(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.9, preserve = "single"),
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("OS" = "dodgerblue", "TBE" = "seagreen3")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 15, by = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 35, by = 5)) +
  labs(#title = "Frequency of sensitivity analyses per study in OS and TBE",
       x = "Number of sensitivity analyses", 
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

It is worth noticing that the number of studies that do not report any sensitivity analysis at all is quite high for both endpoints. 40 studies did not report any sensitivity analysis for OS and 19 did not report any sensitivity analyses for TBE. The fact that $\frac{2}{3}$ of studies did not have any sensitivity analyses for OS is not surprising, as that is considered a more stable and objective endpoint. We then looked at these sensitivity analyses were distributed among the different categories.

The same study could also have multiple sensitivity analyses, which could belong to the same or to different categories. Fig. \@ref(fig:Sensitivity-categories)A shows the number of trials for which different categories of sensitivity analyses, while \@ref(fig:Sensitivity-categories)B illustrates the amount of sensitivity analysis per category across all trials that have been reported in the publicly available documents.

```{r Sensitivity-categories, fig.cap="Sensitivity analyses by endpoint. (A) Number of different sensitivity analysis categories within the same study. (B) Frequency of each sensitivity analysis category per endpoint.", echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
library(patchwork)

## ---------- Panel A ----------
category_summary_TBE <- dif_TBE_clean %>%
  group_by(NCT) %>%
  summarise(n_categories = n_distinct(Type.of.sensitivity.analysis)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_categories))

category_summary_OS <- dif_OS_clean %>%
  group_by(NCT) %>%
  summarise(n_categories = n_distinct(Type.of.sensitivity.analysis)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_categories))

freq_TBE_A <- as.data.frame(table(category_summary_TBE$n_categories))
freq_OS_A  <- as.data.frame(table(category_summary_OS$n_categories))

freq_join_A <- merge(freq_OS_A, freq_TBE_A, by = "Var1", all = TRUE)
freq_join_A[is.na(freq_join_A)] <- 0
colnames(freq_join_A) <- c("Category", "OS", "TBE")

f_long_A <- freq_join_A %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(OS, TBE), names_to = "Endpoint", values_to = "Count")

p_A <- ggplot(f_long_A, aes(x = Category, y = Count, fill = Endpoint)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.65), width = 0.65, color = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, by = 2)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("OS" = "dodgerblue", "TBE" = "seagreen3")) +
  labs(x = "Number of sensitivity analysis categories in the same study",
       y = "Number of studies") +

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1))

## ---------- Panel B ----------
freq_OS_B  <- as.data.frame(table(dif_OS_clean$Type.of.sensitivity.analysis))
freq_TBE_B <- as.data.frame(table(dif_TBE_clean$Type.of.sensitivity.analysis))

freq_join_B <- merge(freq_OS_B, freq_TBE_B, by = "Var1", all = TRUE)
freq_join_B[is.na(freq_join_B)] <- 0
colnames(freq_join_B) <- c("Category", "OS", "TBE")

rel_freq <- freq_join_B
rel_freq[, "TBE"] <- (rel_freq[, "TBE"] / sum(rel_freq["TBE"])) * 100
rel_freq[, "OS"]  <- (rel_freq[, "OS"]  / sum(rel_freq["OS"]))  * 100

f_long_B <- rel_freq %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(OS, TBE), names_to = "Endpoint", values_to = "Count")

p_B <- ggplot(f_long_B, aes(x = Category, y = Count, fill = Endpoint)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.55), width = 0.55, color = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("OS" = "dodgerblue", "TBE" = "seagreen3")) +
  labs(x = "Category", y = "Frequency (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

## ---------- Combine ----------
(p_A | p_B) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 22),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

From this histograms, we can see that most trials (14/17) for OS focus only on one type of category of sensitivity analysis at a time. For TBE it's more common to more different type of analyses, most trials still have only one (16/45) or two (18/45) categories. A deeper look at the category distribution in the different endpoint (Fig. \@ref(fig:Sensitivity-categories)B) shows that, while the sensitivity analyses for TBE mostly focused on different censoring rules (50.78%) and on methods (36.13%), for OS, the focus of the sensitivity analyses was almost entirely on different methods (80.43%), with only 10.87% focusing on censoring and 8.7% focusing on different populations. In the case of TBE, it is worth keeping in mind that different methods also include changes in the way the disease progression is assessed between investigator-based and Independent Central Review (ICR)-based.

### Hazard ratio and standard error comparison

We then focused on examining the possibility of a pattern in the choice of primary and sensitivity analysis. To do so, we compared the logarithm of HRs and the one of the Standard Errors reported in each tria.

Fig. \@ref(fig:Differences-HR-SE)A shows the distribution of $\log(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ while Fig. \@ref(fig:Differences-HR-SE)B illustreate the distribution of $\log(\frac{SE_{Sensitivity}}{SE_{Primary}})$.

```{r Differences-HR-SE, fig.cap="Differences between primary and sensitivity analyses by endpoint. (A) Logarithm of the ratio of hazard ratios. (B) Logarithm of the ratio of standard errors. The dashed red line indicates no difference.", echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
library(patchwork)

## ---------- Panel A: HR ----------
df_HR <- data.frame(
  endpoint  = rep(c("OS", "TBE"), c(length(dif_OS_clean$log_ratio), length(dif_TBE_clean$log_ratio))),
  log_ratio = c(dif_OS_clean$log_ratio, dif_TBE_clean$log_ratio)
)

p_A <- ggplot(df_HR, aes(x = endpoint, y = log_ratio, fill = endpoint)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "endpoint",
                    values = c("OS" = "dodgerblue", "TBE" = "seagreen3")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "firebrick", lwd = 0.7, lty = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +
  ylab("") +
  xlab("")+
  ggtitle("Log ratio of hazard ratios") 

## ---------- Panel B: SE ----------
df_SE <- data.frame(
  endpoint = rep(c("OS", "TBE"), c(length(dif_OS_clean$log_se), length(dif_TBE_clean$log_se))),
  SE       = c(dif_OS_clean$log_se, dif_TBE_clean$log_se)
)

p_B <- ggplot(df_SE, aes(x = endpoint, y = SE, fill = endpoint)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "endpoint",
                    values = c("OS" = "dodgerblue", "TBE" = "seagreen3")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "firebrick", lwd = 0.7, lty = 2) +
  ylab("") +
  xlab("")+
  ggtitle("Log ratio of standard errors") 

## ---------- Combine ----------
(p_A | p_B) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10))
```

From those boxplots we can see that while the logarithm of ratio of HRs in TBE has a median equal to 0 with narrow quartiles, there are more outliers than in OS, whose median is slightly below 0 and has wider quartiles, but no outliers. A similar pattern is visible in the ratio of standard errors, where for TBE has a median slightly below 0 (-0.0055), with narrow quartiles and many outliers, while OS shows more variability but only one outlier. This suggests that the standard errors of sensitivity analyses for OS tend to be larger than the standard errors for the primary analysis. This is not the case for TBE.

To examine the relationship between the differences in HRs and the differences in standard errors, we plotted $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)$ against $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ (Fig. \@ref(fig:Scatter-plot-TBE) for TBE and Fig. \@ref(fig:Scatter-plot-OS))in a scatter plot, where each dot was colored differently according to its NCT, to better visualize the cluster of different trials.

```{r Scatter.plot-TBE, fig.cap="Log ratio of HRs vs ratio of SE for TBE",fig.width=7, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

library(ggplot2)
library(viridis)
library(cowplot)
library(grid)
library(colorspace)
library(ggsci)

fix_column <- function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x) || is.character(x)) {
    suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(x)))
  } else {
    x
  }
}

dif_TBE_clean$log_ratio <- fix_column(dif_TBE_clean$log_ratio)
dif_TBE_clean$log_se <- fix_column(dif_TBE_clean$log_se)
dif_TBE_clean$NCT <- as.factor(dif_TBE_clean$NCT)

# remove rows with missing values
dif_TBE_clean <- subset(dif_TBE_clean, !is.na(log_ratio) & !is.na(log_se) & !is.na(NCT))

library(randomcoloR)
library(ggplot2)

dif_TBE_clean$NCT <- factor(dif_TBE_clean$NCT)
levels_nct <- levels(dif_TBE_clean$NCT)
n <- length(levels_nct)

my_colors <- distinctColorPalette(n)   # returns n distinct colors
names(my_colors) <- levels_nct

# then same ggplot + scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) as above


p_main_TBE <- ggplot(dif_TBE_clean, aes(y = log_ratio, x = log_se, color = NCT)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors)+  # or scale_color_nejm(), scale_color_jama(), etc.
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Logarithm of ratio of Standard Errors", breaks = pretty(dif_TBE_clean$log_se, n = 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Logarithm of the ratio of HR", breaks = pretty(dif_TBE_clean$log_ratio, n = 6)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey85")
  ) +
  labs(title = "TBE")

# ---- Legend-only plot ----
p_legend_TBE <- ggplot(dif_TBE_clean, aes(y = log_ratio, x = log_se, color = NCT)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) + 
  theme_void() +
  guides(color = guide_legend(title = "NCT", ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))

legend_only_TBE <- cowplot::get_legend(p_legend_TBE)

# ---- Print results ----
# Page 1: main plot
p_main_TBE

# Page 2: legend only (will appear below)
cowplot::ggdraw(legend_only_TBE)

```

```{r Scatter.plot-OS, fig.cap="Log ratio of HRs vs ratio of SE for OS" fig.width=7, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
dif_OS_clean$log_ratio <- fix_column(dif_OS_clean$log_ratio)
dif_OS_clean$log_se <- fix_column(dif_OS_clean$log_se)
dif_OS_clean$NCT <- as.factor(dif_OS_clean$NCT)

# remove rows with missing values
dif_OS_clean <- subset(dif_OS_clean, !is.na(log_ratio) & !is.na(log_se) & !is.na(NCT))

# ---- Main plot (no legend) ----
dif_OS_clean$NCT <- factor(dif_OS_clean$NCT)

```

Fig. \@ref(fig:Scatter-plot-TBE) and Fig. \@ref(fig:Scatter-plot-OS) indicates that smaller values of $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)$ correspond to larger values of $\log\left(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)$ and vice versa.

If we consider the hazard ration as $HR=\frac{\frac{O_1}{E_1}}{\frac{O_0}{E_0}}$, where $O_i= Observed\ events \ in \ group \ i$ and $E_i= Expected \ events \ in \ group \ i$ and $SE(log(HR))=\sqrt{\frac{1}{E_1}+ \frac{1}{E_0}}$, the change in the standard errors between primary and sensitivity analyses would indicate that either $E_1$ or $E_0$ has changed. Assuming $\frac{O_1}{O_0}$ has not changed, $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)>0$ indicates that $HR_{Sensitivity}>HR_{Primary}$. Given that higher values of the logarithm of ratio of HRs corresponds also to lower values of the logarithm of ratio of standard errors, this indicates that $E_{0,Sensitivity}>E_{0,Primary}$. Similarly, taking $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)<0$ will indicate $HR_{Sensitivity}<HR_{Primary}$ and given that lower values of the logarithm of ratio of HRs corresponds to higher values of the logarithm of ratio of standard errors, this will indicate that $E_{0,Sensitivity}>E_{0,Primary}$. This would suggest that sensitivity analyses change the expected number event for the control group but not in the treatment group. Since $E_0+E_1=O_0+O_1$, if $E_0$ increase but $E_1$ does not change, that implies that also $O_0+O_1$ also increase, so we should observe more events in the sensitivity analyses than in the primary ones.

### Modelling

This relationship between HRs and standard error differences was further explored through different regression models, to examine the influence that the different categories and that the value of primary HR could have on it.

#### Simple linear models

We initially fitted a linear regression model for each endpoint. **TBE** we obtained the following results:

```{r Linear model TBE, echo=FALSE}
m_TBE=lm(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se, data = dif_TBE_clean)

summ(m_TBE,model.info=FALSE)
confint(m_TBE, level = 0.95)
#tableRegression(m_TBE, xtable = FALSE)

coeff_TBE<-coefficients(m_TBE)            
#intercept_TBE<-coeff_TBE[1]
slope_TBE<- coeff_TBE

p_main_TBE+geom_abline(slope = coeff_TBE, color="black", linetype="dashed", linewidth=0.9)

round(AIC(m_TBE),2)
round(BIC(m_TBE),2)
#summary(m_TBE)
```

There is a significant relationship between the two variables with estimated slope of `r slope_TBE`

This confirms that the ratio in standard errors tends to decrease when the log HR ratio increases, as seen in the scatter plot.

The same model for **OS** gave the following output:

```{r Linear model OS, echo=FALSE}
m_os=lm(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se, data = dif_OS_clean)
summ(m_os,model.info=FALSE)
confint(m_os, level = 0.95)
#tableRegression(m_os, xtable = FALSE)

coeff_OS<-coefficients(m_os)          
#intercept_OS<-coeff_OS[1]
slope_OS<- coeff_OS

p_main_OS+geom_abline(slope = coeff_OS, color="black", linetype="dashed", linewidth=0.9)

round(AIC(m_os),2)
round(BIC(m_os),2)
#summary(m_os)
```

The results for OS seem to show an estimated slope of `r slope_OS` in the same direction as the ones for TBE.

#### Linear model with covariates

To identify the possible causes of the relationship between $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ and $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)$ we expanded the linear model to include the category identifier of the sensitivity analyses as covariate, as they might have an impact on the number of people at risk or on the number of events.

Changing censoring rules could have an impact on both the number of events and of people at risk at various time, modifying both the HR and standard errors. This is because censoring more individuals reduces the number of people at risk and at prevent any event that these individuals might have had to be included in the analysis.

Similarly, using different population for the analysis can also change the relationship between the number of people at risk and the number of events in each arm, which might also impact the standard errors and the HR.

To examine the impact that these changes can have on the analysis we used a linear mixed model that included also the category of sensitivity analysis category as covariate.

To do so we used a dummy variable for each category that would have value 1 if a change in the category was present in the sensitivity analysis and 0 if it did not. This allowed us to consider also the sensitivity analyses that had changes in multiple categories at the same time.

This covariates model for **TBE** gave the following results:

```{r Covariate model TBE, echo=FALSE}
m_TBE_cov=lm(log_ratio ~0+ log_se*Censoring+log_se*Methods+log_se*Population, data = dif_TBE_clean)

summ(m_TBE_cov,model.info=FALSE)
round(AIC(m_TBE_cov),2)
round(BIC(m_TBE_cov),2)
#summary(m_TBE_cov)
```

The results for same model for **OS** were the following:

```{r Covariate model OS, echo=FALSE}
m_os_cov=lm(log_ratio ~0+ log_se*Censoring+log_se*Methods+log_se*Population, data = dif_OS_clean)
summ(m_os_cov,model.info=FALSE)

round(AIC(m_os_cov),2)
round(BIC(m_os_cov),2)
#summary(m_os_cov)
```

From these the results we can see that the category of sensitivity analysis is not relevant neither for *TBE* nor *OS*.

##### Primary HR as regression variable

We explored then the impact of the initial analysis results, including the interaction between $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ and the original HR results for the primary analysis.

The results obtained were the following for *TBE*:

```{r Ref HR as covariate TBE}
mHR_TBE= lm(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se * log(ref_HR), data = dif_TBE_clean)
#mHR_TBE= lm(log_ratio ~ 0+log(ref_HR), data = dif_TBE_clean)
summary(mHR_TBE)
round(AIC(mHR_TBE),2)
round(BIC(mHR_TBE),2)
```

This would suggest that the HR value of the primary analysis has a small impact on the relationship between $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ and $\log\left(\frac{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{HR_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}}\right)$, while the interaction term between the logarithm of the ratio of standard errors has a bigger impact in the other direction but a larger p-value. Similarly the logarithm of the ratio of standard error has a bigger impact, in the same direction of the one of the primary HR, but a larger p-value.

```{r Ref HR as covariate OS}
mHR_OS= lm(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se * log(ref_HR), data = dif_OS_clean) #Remove methods
summary(mHR_OS)
round(AIC(mHR_OS),2)
round(BIC(mHR_OS),2)
```

The results for *OS* presented much larger and non-significant p-values for both the interaction term and the primary HR one, but it also presents a strong significance and a stronger negative coefficient for the logarithm of the ratio of standard errors.

#### Random effect models

Since multiple points of the dataset come from the same RCT, we also fitted a random effect model with the RCT ID as random intercept, in order to take into account the effect that this clustering could have on the analysis

We initially run a simple model with random intercept for each trial.

For the different **TBE**, the results are:

```{r Random model TBE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(performance)
library(lme4)
r_model_TBE=lmer(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se+(1|NCT), data = dif_TBE_clean)

su=as.data.frame(summary(r_model_TBE)$varcor)
ICC_TBE=(su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2/((su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2+(su[su$grp=="Residual", "sdcor"])**2)

summ(r_model_TBE, model.info=FALSE)

# Fitted vs observed correlation squared
fitted_vals <- fitted(r_model_TBE)
r2_manual <- cor(fitted_vals, dif_TBE_clean$log_se)^2
r2(r_model_TBE)
```

For **OS** the random effect model shows the following results:

```{r Random model OS,warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

r_model_OS=lmer(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se+ (1 | NCT), data = dif_OS_clean)
su=as.data.frame(summary(r_model_OS)$varcor)
ICC_OS=(su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2/((su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2+(su[su$grp=="Residual", "sdcor"])**2)
summ(r_model_OS,model.info=FALSE)
fitted_vals <- fitted(r_model_OS)
r2_manual <- cor(fitted_vals, dif_OS_clean$log_se)^2
r2(r_model_OS)
```

For both endpoints the results are very close to the one we obtained for the simple linear regression model.

Then we included the HR of the primary analysis as a covariate.

```{r Random model SE TBE}
r_model_TBE_se=lmer(log_ratio ~0+log_se * log(ref_HR)+(1|NCT), data = dif_TBE_clean)
su=as.data.frame(summary(r_model_TBE_se)$varcor)
ICC_OS=(su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2/((su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2+(su[su$grp=="Residual", "sdcor"])**2)
summ(r_model_TBE_se,model.info=FALSE)
fitted_vals <- fitted(r_model_TBE_se)
r2_manual <- cor(fitted_vals, dif_TBE_clean$log_se)^2
r2(r_model_TBE_se)
```

The results for this random model for *TBE* show that, when accounting for trial provenance using random intercepts, the impact of $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ itself decreases while its p-value increases becoming non-significant, but the impact of the interaction between the primary analysis HR and $\log(\frac{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Sensitivity}}}{SE_{\scriptsize \mbox{Primary}}})$ increases and its p-value becomes very small.

```{r}
r_model_OS_se=lmer(log_ratio ~ 0+log_se * log(ref_HR)+(1|NCT), data = dif_OS_clean)
su=as.data.frame(summary(r_model_OS_se)$varcor)
ICC_OS=(su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2/((su[su$grp=="NCT", "sdcor"])**2+(su[su$grp=="Residual", "sdcor"])**2)
summ(r_model_OS_se,model.info=FALSE)
fitted_vals <- fitted(r_model_OS_se)
r2_manual <- cor(fitted_vals, dif_OS_clean$log_se)^2
r2(r_model_OS_se)
```

We did not obtain the same type of results for *OS*, but this endpoint also has a much smaller sample size (46 for OS vs 191 data points for TBE) so it has a considerably larger standard error because of a smaller sample size and an increased residual variance. Also there were only few studies that had more than 1 sensitivity analysis for *OS.*

## Discussion

In this exploratory analysis, we examined whether the difference in standard errors of between sensitivity and primary analysis in oncological RCTs was associated with a change in the effect estimate.

Both the simple linear model and the scatter plot indicated a relationship between the ratio of standard errors and the ratio of HRs (-0,66 with 95% CI [-0.82,-0.51] for TBE and -0.22 and 95% Ci [-0.33,-0,12] for OS). Sensitivity analyses with smaller standard errors in the sensitivity analyses tended to report larger HRs , which is something we would expect if the type of analysis affected the amount of events of population included in the analysis.

To explore what might cause this relationship, we added the category of the sensitivity analysis and the original value of HR as covariates in the model. None of the covariates we included was significantly associated with the ratio of HRs, so we could not identify a specific trial characteristics to explain the pattern. This might also reflect some limitations of this study, which might have limited power to detect smaller effects.

Because most trials reported more than one sensitivity analysis per endpoint and therefore the data points were not strictly independent, we repeated the analyses accounting for clustering of sensitivity analyses withing trials using mixed-effects model with random intercepts for each trial. The results obtained were similar to the ones yield by the simple linear models, which suggests that the pattern is not driven by the non-independence of the data points. However, since most trials only reported few sensitivity analysis, the estimation of the between-trial variability might be imprecise.

Overall these findings suggest that the difference in HRs between primary and sensitivity analyses are consistent with differences in the standard errors between them, but given the limitations of this study, further research on this association is needed.

## Limitations

This study presents several limitations.

Firstly, it is an exploratory component of a larger reproducibility study, therefore the sample size was determined to obtain adequate power for the primary reproducibility objective. As a result this part of the study might lack the necessary power to detect more modest associations between trial characteristics and the ratio of HRs, therefore the absence of significant effects should not be interpreted as evidence of a lack of association. Also any significant findings would also need to be interpreted carefully because of multiplicity.

Another limitation is that our analyses relies on the numerical results reported on publicly available documents (EPARs, publications and their supplementary materials). It is possible the trials explored have conducted additional sensitivity analyses that were not reported in the documents we extracted our data from. This could bias our estimate in either direction as we do not know if the non-reported sensitivity analysis results differ systematically from the reported ones.

## Conclusions

The 60 randomly selected studies that we analysed in this project gave us an idea on the use of sensitivity analyses in oncological RCTs. Even if sensitivity analyses are a very useful practice, especially when dealing with tumor-based endpoints, which are more prone to subjectivity and bias, they are still not planned, nor reported for many studies. The analyses that were reported employed mostly different censoring rules than those used in the primary analysis, and a lower number of them also focused on the different methods and assessment strategies. When comparing these sensitivity analyses with the primary, it was possible to see some effect of Hazard Ratios on the Standard errors. More specifically the analyses we run seemed to point at a relationship between the original value of HR for the primary analysis and a change in the standard errors of sensitivity analyses.

Further assessment on new samples of studies would be needed to confirm this hypothesis.
